record.title: Human screen takeover (safety override) blocks behind an untimed agent GUI exec holding gui_lock while the in-container X server is unresponsive
record.description: Agent GUI tools (screenshot/click/type/key) run through AgentBox._run_tool, which acquires desktop.gui_lock(sid) and calls SandboxManager._x -> docker exec_run (scrot/xdotool) with no container-side timeout wrapper, unlike exec (timeout -k 5), read_file and outbox_read (timeout -k 2 30). takeover and handback acquire the same plain threading.Lock via `with`, with no acquisition deadline. If the X server stops answering while an agent GUI exec is outstanding, that exec blocks inside the held lock, so the human takeover (the safety override for a misbehaving screen) and handback queue behind it. Source chain verified at the cited lines; gui_lock is a plain threading.Lock (desktop.py:155-158). Parent-live evidence (the parent's, not the verifier's; no Docker here): l1_takeover.py SIGSTOPs Xvfb (uid desktop=1001) in a real desktop sandbox, issues an agent screenshot that hangs holding gui_lock, then starts a takeover: it does not return within 20 s. l10_bound.py (after Phase 3) ran the same setup for 150 s: after 151 s both the screenshot and the takeover were still blocked, and both returned only after SIGCONT (screenshot 153 s, takeover 151 s). So the hang is not capped by the docker SDK client timeout and the lock is not released by a ReadTimeout, which settles the bound: the lockout lasts as long as X stays unresponsive. Not yet established: that a prompt-injected agent, using only its own agent-token capabilities, can itself make X unresponsive. The parent's SIGSTOP was a docker exec as uid 1001, standing in for a GUI terminal step (N-1). Source makes it plausible: the type/key tools can drive xfce4-terminal (Dockerfile:19), which runs as the same uid as Xvfb, and a process may signal another process of its own uid.
record.claimed_root_cause: gui_lock is held across SandboxManager._x exec_run with no container-side timeout wrapper (unlike exec/read_file/outbox_read, which use `timeout -k`), and takeover/handback acquire the same plain threading.Lock unconditionally with no acquisition deadline, so a hung GUI exec serializes the human safety override behind it for as long as the in-container X server is unresponsive.

trace.description: Lowest-trust agent token POSTs a GUI tool (screenshot/click/type/key) to /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/{tool}, dispatched on tool_pool.
For GUI tools, acquires `with self.desktop.gui_lock(sid):` and runs the GUI method while holding it.
Runs c.exec_run(argv, user=desktop, ...) for scrot/xdotool with no container-side `timeout -k` wrapper, so the exec blocks for as long as X is unresponsive.
Human takeover (safety override) acquires the same gui_lock via a plain `with` (no deadline) and cannot return until the hung GUI exec releases it.

evidence.description: `with self.desktop.gui_lock(sid):` wraps the entire GUI tool execution in _run_tool.
_x returns c.exec_run(argv, user=DESKTOP_USER, environment=DESKTOP_ENV, demux=True) with no `timeout -k` wrapper.
By contrast, exec wraps argv in a container-side `timeout -k 5 <t>`; read_file (561) and outbox_read (665) use `timeout -k 2 30`; _x has no equivalent bound.
self.client = docker.from_env() with no explicit timeout; parent-live l10 shows the exec still blocked at 151 s, so this client default does not bound the hang.
handback also acquires gui_lock via a plain `with`, unconditionally and with no acquisition deadline.
takeover acquires gui_lock with the inline comment that it waits until the running GUI tool finishes; no timeout/409 path.
gui_lock(sid) returns self._gui.setdefault(sid, threading.Lock()), a plain threading.Lock acquired only via `with` (no timeout) everywhere it is used.
`as_desktop Xvfb :0 ...` runs the X server as uid 1001 (desktop), the same account as GUI-launched programs.
The desktop image ships xfce4-terminal, so the agent's key/type tools (sandbox.py:740, 749) can reach a shell running as uid 1001, the same uid as Xvfb.

Parent-live: with Xvfb stopped, after 151 s the agent screenshot and the human takeover were both still blocked; they returned only after SIGCONT (153 s / 151 s). Stand-in: the stop was done by docker exec as uid 1001, not by the agent.

blockers: Whether a prompt-injected agent, using only its own agent-token calls (key/type/click to open a GUI terminal as uid 1001 and run e.g. `kill -STOP $(pgrep -x Xvfb)`), can itself make the in-container X server unresponsive so that a following agent GUI call hangs holding gui_lock. The parent-live runs (l1_takeover.py, l10_bound.py) induced the stall with a docker-exec SIGSTOP as uid 1001 as a stand-in for that GUI step. It decides between an agent-triggerable lockout of the human override and an owner-induced X freeze, and needs the live Docker daemon and agentbox-desktop:0.1.

validation_plan.local: Disposable desktop sandbox on a real Docker daemon with agentbox-desktop:0.1 (loopback only, dummy tokens), driven only through box.call_tool / POST /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/{tool} with the agent token (no docker exec after create): (1) call key `ctrl+alt+t` (or click the panel terminal launcher), then type `kill -STOP $(pgrep -x Xvfb)` followed by key `Return`; (2) issue one agent screenshot and record whether it hangs; (3) start a takeover from a UI session and record whether it returns within 60 s. Then SIGCONT Xvfb with docker exec as cleanup and record the elapsed times. If the keybinding fails, use an equivalent agent-reachable step (panel launcher click). A pass reproduces the l10 result with no owner-side signal and promotes the record to confirmed. Fix check: wrap _x argv in a container-side `timeout -k 2 N` as exec/read_file/outbox_read do, and have takeover/handback use gui_lock.acquire(timeout=...) returning 409/503 on contention so the human override is never serialized unboundedly behind an agent GUI exec.
